title: Forward collision warning and autonomous emergency braking cut rates of rear-end crashes by up to 50% in 22 U.S. states, and the federal safety regulator cites the finding for a braking mandate
summary: In an Insurance Institute for Highway Safety study, forward collision warning alone, low-speed emergency braking and warning with braking cut rear-end striking crash rates by 27%, 43% and 50%.
account: Jessica Cicchino of the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety measured police-reported crash involvements per insured vehicle year in 22 U.S. states during 2010–2014. She compared passenger vehicle models with optional forward collision warning alone, or with forward collision warning and autonomous emergency braking, to the same models without these systems. She also compared Volvo 2011–2012 S60 and 2010–2012 XC60 vehicles, which had standard low-speed autonomous emergency braking, to other luxury midsize cars and sport utility vehicles without it. She published the study in Accident Analysis and Prevention volume 99 in February 2017. Forward collision warning alone, low-speed autonomous emergency braking and warning with braking reduced rear-end striking crash involvement rates by 27%, 43% and 50%. Injury crash rates fell 20%, 45% and 56%. Warning with braking increased rear-end struck involvements by 20%. No individual avoided crash is documented. In its proposed rule of 13 June 2023, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration cited this study and adopted its finding that forward collision warning cut rear-end crashes by 27 percent. On 9 May 2024 the agency adopted a final rule that makes autonomous emergency braking mandatory on new light vehicles from 1 September 2029. On 17 January 2025 Auto Innovators, an industry group, asked the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit to review the rule. The case has been on hold since February 2025. On 23 March 2026 the Department of Transportation told the court that it is preparing a proposal to amend the rule. On 22 April 2026 the National Law Review reported that the proposal would extend the compliance lead time by two years.
purpose: Built to warn drivers and brake automatically when a frontal collision is imminent. The measured reduction in rear-end striking crashes is the intended benefit.
system: Front crash prevention systems (FCW, low-speed AEB, FCW with AEB) on passenger vehicles from multiple automakers, including Volvo's standard low-speed AEB on 2011–2012 S60 and 2010–2012 XC60

ratings.reason: Across insured vehicles in 22 states, rates of rear-end striking crashes fell 27%, 43% and 50% for the three system types, and rates of those crashes with injuries fell 20%, 45% and 56%. This is a change documented across a vehicle population. The study does not report the severity of the injuries.
The study reports cohort-level rate reductions without individually attributable outcomes.

ai_role.statement: Front crash prevention systems are automated perception-and-braking systems. The within-model comparisons (FCW alone, FCW with AEB) and Volvo S60/XC60 comparison with other luxury midsize cars and SUVs (low-speed AEB) control for other factors. They show effectiveness as a rate, not any single avoided crash. Whether such systems count as AI is a definitional choice the sources do not settle.

fields.summary: In an Insurance Institute for Highway Safety study, forward collision warning alone, low-speed emergency braking and warning with braking cut rear-end striking crash rates by 27%, 43% and 50%.
fields.account: Jessica Cicchino of the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety measured police-reported crash involvements per insured vehicle year in 22 U.S. states during 2010–2014. She compared passenger vehicle models with optional forward collision warning alone, or with forward collision warning and autonomous emergency braking, to the same models without these systems. She also compared Volvo 2011–2012 S60 and 2010–2012 XC60 vehicles, which had standard low-speed autonomous emergency braking, to other luxury midsize cars and sport utility vehicles without it. She published the study in Accident Analysis and Prevention volume 99 in February 2017. Forward collision warning alone, low-speed autonomous emergency braking and warning with braking reduced rear-end striking crash involvement rates by 27%, 43% and 50%. Injury crash rates fell 20%, 45% and 56%. Warning with braking increased rear-end struck involvements by 20%. No individual avoided crash is documented. In its proposed rule of 13 June 2023, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration cited this study and adopted its finding that forward collision warning cut rear-end crashes by 27 percent. On 9 May 2024 the agency adopted a final rule that makes autonomous emergency braking mandatory on new light vehicles from 1 September 2029. On 17 January 2025 Auto Innovators, an industry group, asked the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit to review the rule. The case has been on hold since February 2025. On 23 March 2026 the Department of Transportation told the court that it is preparing a proposal to amend the rule. On 22 April 2026 the National Law Review reported that the proposal would extend the compliance lead time by two years.
